title: Disorders of white blood cells
covers: Non-malignant WBC disorders: leukocytosis and its forms, leukemoid and leukoerythroblastic reactions, neutropenia (ANC grades, drug, infection, congenital, immune, margination), lymphopenia, and neutrophil function defects (LAD, Chediak-Higashi, CGD).

ul: Adult WBC 4,000–11,000/µL (4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L). Know the normal ranges for age before calling a count abnormal.
About 90% of WBCs sit in the marrow, 2–3% circulate, 7–8% are in tissues. WBC life span 11–16 days, mostly in the marrow.
The marrow pool can raise circulating WBCs 2–3-fold within a few hours.
Neutrophils are ~60% of adult WBCs: 9 days in the marrow, 3–6 hours in blood, 1–4 days in tissue.
Circulating neutrophils are either free or marginated on the vessel wall (~50% marginated). A shift between the two pools changes the count without any new production.
Recruitment: chemoattractant → rolling → activation → adhesion → migration → phagocytosis → killing. Selectins sit on endothelial cells, integrins on neutrophils.
Killing tools: reactive oxygen species, secreted toxic molecules, proteases, phagocytosis.
Lymphoblasts give B cells (→ plasma cells), T cells (via the thymus) and NK cells.

items.p: Myeloblast → promyelocyte → myelocyte → metamyelocyte → band → segmented neutrophil.

With maturation, cell size, nuclear volume and nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio fall. Chromatin goes from fine and round to dark and segmented. Granules go from none to primary (azurophilic) to specific (secondary).

table: Qualitative (hereditary or acquired, permanent or transient)

items.p: Leukocytosis = WBC > 11,000/µL (or > 2 SD above the mean) in adults. Mostly neutrophilia, then lymphocytosis.
Always work from absolute counts: WBC × percentage.

table: WBC > 50,000/µL, not from leukemia (rule leukemia out first)
Sludging of very many leukocytes in small vessels; can kill (blood flow, metabolic demand)

items.note: The slides write several counts as "/mL" (slides 3, 14, 20, 26, 27); the values are per µL. Slide 14 also calls the leukemoid reaction "hyperleukocytosis"; in standard use hyperleukocytosis means WBC > 100,000/µL, usually in leukemia. Slide 15 defines the leukoerythroblastic reaction as a leukemoid reaction plus nucleated RBCs; standard sources define it by immature granulocytes plus nucleated RBCs, whatever the total count.

ul: History: fever (duration, degree, cause), B symptoms, fatigue, bleeding, bone pain, past infections, poor wound healing, drugs, toxins, travel, exercise, smoking, stress, asplenia, a previous CBC, family history.
Exam: vital signs, pallor, infection focus (tonsils, lungs, heart murmur), rash, joints, nodes, liver and spleen, masses, petechiae, dysmorphic or skeletal features.
Causes: infections, inflammation, drugs, marrow disorders, immune disorders; also exercise, pregnancy, smoking, asplenia, stress, trauma, hemolysis.

Suspect a marrow disorder: weight loss, bruising, pallor, recurrent life-threatening infections, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, very high WBC, abnormal RBC or platelet counts, blasts on the smear.
Emergency: clinical instability (hypotension, high fever, hypothermia, rebound tenderness), blasts with DIC, WBC > 100,000/µL.

table: Viral titers, cultures, stool for parasites, chest X-ray, echocardiography
Bone marrow exam ± imaging, flow cytometry, cytogenetics, molecular studies

summary.h: Neutrophilia, lymphocytosis and the other increases

ul: Neutrophilia: reactive is most common (infection, inflammation, drugs, immune). Marrow causes: myeloproliferative disorders (CML, ET, PV, CMML, CNL, JMML), hereditary neutrophilia (LAD), chronic idiopathic neutrophilia. Demargination also raises the count.
Case: 3-year-old with pneumonia, WBC 34,000/µL, neutrophils 73%, bands 8% → severe bacterial infection with a responding marrow. Raised bands = left shift. Recovered in 48 hours.

Lymphocytosis (> 4,000/µL; can be normal under 2 years): viruses are the most common cause (EBV, CMV, HIV, HTLV-1, influenza, hepatitis, mumps, measles, rubella); selected bacteria (pertussis, TB, brucellosis, syphilis); parasites (toxoplasmosis, malaria); CLL (elderly, with anemia, low platelets or neutrophils, splenomegaly); occasionally NHL; stress, drugs, asplenia.

Infectious mononucleosis: acute EBV in adolescents and young adults. Fever, fatigue, sore throat, exudative tonsillitis, splenomegaly. High WBC with atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells), positive EBV-specific antibody test. Self-limited; supportive care.
Eosinophilia (> 500/µL): allergies, parasites, some cancers. Case: 8-year-old with eczema, wheeze and 20% eosinophils → asthma.
Monocytosis (> 800/µL): infections, inflammation, rarely cancer. Basophilia (> 200/µL): allergies, inflammation, myeloproliferative disorders.

items.p: Neutropenia is the major cause of leukopenia (causes: infections, drugs, marrow failure, immune).

table: Drugs, infections, irradiation and toxins, marrow failure syndromes
Infections, drugs, immune (SLE, RA, neonatal alloimmune)
Severe infection or endotoxin, hemodialysis, cardiopulmonary bypass

ul: Neutropenia itself gives no symptoms; it is suspected from frequent or unusual infections.
Severe neutropenia: fatigue, sleeplessness, restlessness, headache, high fever and chills, sore mouth and throat, skin and visceral infections, abscesses.
Agranulocytosis: life-threatening infection (shock, DIC). Severe neutropenia, agranulocytosis and WBC > 100 ×10⁹/L are emergencies.

items.note: Slide 30 sets leukopenia at WBC < 4.4 ×10⁹/L, while slide 3 gives a normal range from 4.0. The cut-off was not tested.

ul: Drugs (very frequent; mild to agranulocytosis; dose-related or idiosyncratic):

Case: 16-year-old who took a pill for low mood, then fever and stomatitis, ANC 0.3 → 0.2 ×10⁹/L, normal Hb, platelets and indices → drug-induced (normal indices rule out megaloblastic anemia, normal Hb and platelets rule out aplastic anemia, persistence rules out margination).

Infections: viruses (HIV, CMV, EBV, HPV, RSV, parvovirus B19, hepatitis, influenza, herpes, measles, rubella, varicella), bacteria (salmonella, brucella, shigella, TB), rickettsia, malaria. Case: typhoid fever with ANC 1.4 and platelets 90. Ask: is the infection due to neutropenia, or the neutropenia due to infection?

Severe congenital neutropenia: rare (1–2 per million). ANC < 0.5 to < 0.2 ×10⁹/L, marrow maturation arrest at the promyelocyte–myelocyte stage, early life-threatening infections, predisposition to leukemia. ELA2 (neutrophil elastase 2) in most cases. Treatment: G-CSF, stem cell transplant. Case: 1-week-old of consanguineous parents, S. aureus cellulitis, ANC 0 that persists → bone marrow aspirate.
Immune neutropenia: the most likely cause of isolated neutropenia. Antibody or cytotoxic T cell mediated; coated neutrophils are removed by the RE system.

table: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta against neutrophil antigens inherited from the father
Granulocyte autoantibodies; with infections, collagen vascular disease, immune deficiency
No cause found; a diagnosis of exclusion

items.p: In unexplained neutropenia, exclude myelodysplastic syndrome and marrow infiltration.
Most cases need no treatment. Otherwise treat by cause:

table: Stop it; teach urgent review for fever or mouth sores
Treat the disease plus supportive care
Urgent admission, broad-spectrum antibiotics, cultures, blood products, G-CSF

ul: Lymphopenia: < 1.5 ×10⁹/L in adults, < 3.0 in children. Major causes: immune deficiencies, malnutrition. Others: steroids, chemotherapy, marrow failure, TB, Hodgkin lymphoma.
Case: 9-month-old with ear discharge, diarrhea, failure to thrive, absent tonsils and lymph nodes, low lymphocytes → severe combined immunodeficiency.
Eosinopenia (< 0.04 ×10⁹/L): acute stress, acute inflammation, corticosteroids.
Basopenia: corticosteroids, stress, acute inflammation, hyperthyroidism, acute hypersensitivity, infections.
Monocytopenia: in the first hours after prednisone, then recovers.

items.note: Slide 48 sets basopenia at < 0.1 ×10⁹/L (the usual basophil count is already about 0–0.1) and says monocytes recover by 12 hours after prednisone (many sources: about 24 hours). Neither number was tested. Slide 47 calls a lymphocyte count of 3.0 ×10⁹/L low, exactly at the child cut-off.

ul: Adhesion: LAD I, LAD II. Chemotaxis: LAD I, Chediak-Higashi, hyper-IgE (Job), actin defects, aggressive periodontitis. Phagocytosis: LAD I, actin defects. Killing: CGD, Chediak-Higashi, specific granule deficiency, neutrophil G6PD deficiency.

Clues: chronic skin and mucosal infections, omphalitis, scarring; indolent node, lung or liver infections; unusual microbes (Serratia, Nocardia, Aspergillus, Pseudomonas), mainly in CGD; less overt sepsis than in severe neutropenia; no abscesses when migration fails; low-grade fevers with hard-to-culture organisms.

table: CD18/11. Type I: no β2 integrins (ITGB2). Type II: no selectin ligands (SLC35C1). Type III: β integrins fail in leukocytes and platelets (FERMT3)
Leukocytosis, delayed cord separation, poor wound healing, severe bacterial infections
CHS1/LYST lysosomal trafficking regulator; granule fusion defect
Partial albinism, nystagmus, giant leukocyte granules, platelets lack dense granules, some neutropenia
Bacterial and fungal infections, granulomas, poor growth, lung disease, autoimmunity
Treat infections early, lifelong antimicrobial prophylaxis, HSCT if high risk

items.p: CGD is diagnosed by neutrophil function testing and mutation analysis.

items.note: Slide 53 says LAD has "4 types" but lists three. Not tested.
ELA2 is now usually called ELANE (outside the slides).

cards.q: Where are most WBCs, and how fast can the blood count rise?
cards.a: ~90% in the marrow (2–3% blood, 7–8% tissue); 2–3-fold rise within hours

Myeloblast → promyelocyte → myelocyte → metamyelocyte → band → segmented neutrophil

cards.q: What fraction of blood neutrophils is marginated?
cards.a: ~50%; shifting them into circulation raises the count without new production
Rolling (selectins on endothelium) → activation → adhesion (integrins on neutrophil) → migration → phagocytosis → killing

cards.a: WBC > 50,000/µL not due to leukemia (trauma, infection, drugs); rule out leukemia first
Sludging of very high leukocyte numbers in small vessels in leukemia; can be fatal
Immature white cells plus nucleated RBCs; myelofibrosis, metastatic cancer, severe hemolysis

cards.a: Weight loss, bruising, pallor, life-threatening infections, organomegaly, nodes, very high WBC, abnormal RBC/platelets, blasts
Clinical instability, blasts with DIC, or WBC > 100,000/µL
Viral infection; also pertussis, TB, toxoplasmosis, CLL; can be normal under 2 years
Atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells); EBV-specific antibody test; supportive

cards.q: Causes of eosinophilia and of basophilia
cards.a: Eosinophilia: allergy, parasites, some cancers. Basophilia: allergy, inflammation, myeloproliferative disorders.
Mild 1.0–2.0, moderate 0.5–1.0, severe < 0.5, agranulocytosis < 0.1 ×10⁹/L
Decreased production, increased destruction, sequestration (spleen, hemangioma), shift to the marginating pool
DNA synthesis: hydroxyurea, phenothiazines, chloramphenicol. Complement-mediated: antithyroid drugs, sulfas, NSAIDs.

cards.q: Causes of margination neutropenia, and its treatment
cards.a: Severe infection/endotoxin, hemodialysis, cardiopulmonary bypass; none needed
Maturation arrest at promyelocyte–myelocyte; ELA2; early severe infections; leukemia risk; G-CSF, SCT

Maternal IgG against neutrophil antigens inherited from the father

cards.a: Myelodysplastic syndrome and marrow infiltration; chronic idiopathic neutropenia is a diagnosis of exclusion
Urgent admission, broad-spectrum antibiotics, cultures, blood products, G-CSF
< 1.5 adults, < 3.0 children (×10⁹/L); immune deficiency, malnutrition

cards.q: What do corticosteroids do to eosinophils, basophils and monocytes?
cards.a: Lower all three (monocytes only for the first hours)
I: no β2 integrins (CD18). II: no selectin ligands. III: β integrins fail in leukocytes and platelets (bleeding).
LYST defect; partial albinism, nystagmus, giant granules, platelets lack dense granules; SCT
NADPH oxidase defect, no superoxide; bacterial and fungal infections, granulomas; neutrophil function test; lifelong prophylaxis

questions.stem: A 1-year-old has a routine CBC: WBC 11,500/µL with 62% lymphocytes. The report flags lymphocytosis against adult ranges. He is well and his examination is normal. What is the best interpretation?
questions.explanation: Know the normal ranges for age before deciding a WBC count is abnormal. Lymphocytosis (adult cut-off > 4,000/µL) can be a normal finding in children under 2 years. A: He is well; a high lymphocyte share is normal under 2 years. B: A disease of the elderly. C: No cough. D: Needs WBC > 50,000/µL.

questions.stem: Where are about 90% of the body's white blood cells at any given time?
questions.explanation: About 90% of WBCs stay in the bone marrow, 2–3% circulate and 7–8% are in tissues; the WBC life span (11–16 days) is mostly spent in the marrow. A: About 2–3%. B: About 7–8%. C: Not the main pool. E: Not the main pool.

questions.stem: A man with pneumonia has a WBC count of 6,000/µL in the morning and 15,000/µL by the evening. What best explains so fast a rise?
questions.explanation: The marrow WBC pool responds rapidly to demand, with a 2–3-fold increase in circulating WBCs within a few hours. A: Production takes days (9 days in the marrow). B: Not the main reserve. D: Lymphocytes, not neutrophils. E: Not the mechanism described.

questions.stem: Which cell comes directly before the band neutrophil in granulopoiesis?
questions.explanation: Myeloblast → promyelocyte → myelocyte → metamyelocyte → band → segmented neutrophil. A: Comes before the metamyelocyte. C: Comes before the myelocyte. D: The first stage. E: Comes after the band.

questions.stem: As a myeloblast matures into a segmented neutrophil, which change occurs?

options.E: Specific granules appear before primary ones

questions.explanation: With maturation, cell size and nuclear volume decrease, round fine chromatin becomes segmented and dark, the nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio decreases, and granules go from none to primary (azurophilic) to specific (secondary). B: Cell size generally decreases. C: It goes from fine to dark and segmented. D: It generally decreases. E: Primary (azurophilic) granules come first.

questions.stem: About what share of the white cells in a healthy adult are neutrophils?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are around 60% of adult WBCs. They attack, ingest and digest microbes using reactive oxygen species, secreted toxic molecules, proteases and phagocytosis. A: Too low. B: Too low. C: Too high. E: Too low.

questions.stem: How long does a neutrophil usually spend in the circulating blood?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils have a larger pool and longer life cycle in the marrow (9 days) than in blood (3–6 hours) and tissue (1–4 days). A: Time in the marrow. B: Time in the tissues. C: The whole WBC life span. D: Too long.

questions.stem: Which mechanism raises the blood neutrophil count without any new marrow production?
questions.explanation: The circulating pool has a freely circulating part and a marginating (vessel wall) part. A shift of neutrophils from the marginating to the circulating pool raises the count. B: That is new production. C: Does not return cells to blood. D: Lowers the count. E: Lowers the count.

questions.stem: About what share of blood neutrophils are reversibly adherent to the endothelium?
questions.explanation: About 50% of neutrophils are reversibly adherent to the endothelium (marginated). A: Too low. B: Too low. D: Too high. E: The share of WBCs kept in the marrow.

questions.stem: In neutrophil recruitment to infected tissue, which step comes directly after rolling?
questions.explanation: Chemoattractant from damaged tissue → attachment/rolling → activation → adhesion → migration → phagocytosis → killing. A: Follows activation. C: Follows adhesion. D: Happens at the site. E: The last step.

questions.stem: During firm adhesion of a white cell to the vessel wall, on which cell are the binding integrins expressed?
questions.explanation: Migration of WBCs to inflamed sites is mediated by adhesion molecules on both cells: selectins on endothelial cells and integrins on neutrophils. A: Carries the selectins. B: Not in this step. C: Not in this step. E: Outside the vessel.

questions.stem: Which lymphoid cell completes its maturation in the thymus?
questions.explanation: Lymphoblasts give rise to B lymphocytes (which become plasma cells), T lymphocytes (via the thymus) and natural killer cells. A: Marrow-derived; becomes a plasma cell. B: Comes from the B lymphocyte. C: Not thymic. D: The precursor.

questions.stem: During a severe illness, a patient's neutrophils fail to migrate normally. The neutrophil count is normal, and function returns after recovery. How is this disorder best classified?

options.E: A shift to the marginating pool

questions.explanation: Non-malignant WBC disorders are quantitative (leukocytosis, leukopenia) or qualitative. Qualitative disorders may be hereditary or acquired, permanent or transient. B: Would be permanent. C: Malignant; raises counts. D: The count is normal. E: Changes the count, not function.

questions.stem: In adults, leukocytosis is most often due to an increase in which cell?
questions.explanation: Leukocytosis (WBC > 2 SD above the mean or > 11,000/µL in adults) is mostly due to neutrophilia, followed by lymphocytosis. A: The second most common. B: Less common. D: Less common. E: Least common.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old has WBC 9,000/µL: neutrophils 55%, lymphocytes 30%, monocytes 12%, eosinophils 2%, basophils 1%. Which abnormality is present?
questions.explanation: Absolute monocyte count = 9,000 × 0.12 = 1,080/µL, above 800/µL: monocytosis, even with a normal total WBC. A: 9,000/µL is normal. C: 4,950/µL, below 7,500. D: 2,700/µL, below 4,000. E: 180/µL, below 500.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old has WBC 12,000/µL: neutrophils 52%, lymphocytes 40%, monocytes 5%, eosinophils 2%, basophils 1%. Which absolute count is raised?
questions.explanation: Absolute lymphocyte count = 4,800/µL, above 4,000/µL in adults: lymphocytosis. A: 6,240/µL, below 7,500. B: 600/µL, below 800. C: 240/µL, below 500. D: 120/µL, below 200.

questions.stem: In an adult, basophilia is an absolute basophil count above what value?
questions.explanation: Adult cut-offs: neutrophilia > 7,500, lymphocytosis > 4,000, monocytosis > 800, eosinophilia > 500, basophilia > 200/µL. A: Eosinophilia. B: Monocytosis. D: Lymphocytosis. E: Neutrophilia.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with severe pneumonia has WBC 58,000/µL, mostly segmented neutrophils and bands, with no blasts. What is this picture called?
questions.explanation: Leukemoid reaction: WBC > 50,000/µL from causes other than leukemia (trauma, infections, drugs). B: Sludging of leukemic cells. C: Needs nucleated red cells. D: A cause is evident. E: Leukemia; a reactive cause is evident.

questions.stem: Before a leukemoid reaction can be diagnosed, which condition must be ruled out?
questions.explanation: Leukemoid reaction is seen in trauma, infections and drugs; before making this diagnosis it is important to rule out leukemia. A: A cause of leukemoid reaction. C: A cause of leukemoid reaction. D: A cause of leukemoid reaction. E: A cause of mild leukocytosis.

questions.stem: A man with newly diagnosed leukemia has a WBC of 250,000/µL and becomes confused and short of breath. What is the mechanism?

options.A: Shift of cells to the marginating pool
options.D: Sludging of leukocytes in small vessels

questions.explanation: Leukostasis (seen in leukemia) results from sludging of high numbers of leukocytes in small blood vessels; it can kill through impaired blood flow or increased metabolic requirements. WBC > 100,000/µL is an emergency. A: Lowers the count. B: Causes neutropenia. C: Leukoerythroblastic picture. E: LAD.

questions.stem: A woman with metastatic breast cancer has immature granulocytes and nucleated red cells on her blood smear. What is this picture called?

options.E: Reactive neutrophilia with a left shift

questions.explanation: Leukoerythroblastic reaction: leukemoid reaction plus increased nucleated RBCs; seen in myelofibrosis, metastatic cancer and severe hemolysis. A: No nucleated red cells. C: Sludging in leukemia. D: Atypical lymphocytes. E: No nucleated red cells.

questions.stem: Which condition can produce a leukoerythroblastic reaction?
questions.explanation: Leukoerythroblastic reaction (immature white cells plus nucleated RBCs) is seen in myelofibrosis, metastatic cancer and severe hemolysis. A: Eosinophilia. B: Neutropenia. C: Shift to the marginating pool. D: Lymphocytosis.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has fever and a WBC of 14,000/µL. Which item of history best tells whether the leukocytosis is new?
questions.explanation: The history covers fever, B symptoms, past infections, wound healing, medications, toxins, travel, exercise, smoking, stress, asplenia, a previous CBC and family history. Only an earlier CBC shows when the high count started. B: Points to a cause. C: Points to a cause. D: Points to a cause. E: Points to a hereditary cause.

questions.stem: Which examination finding in a febrile patient with leukocytosis points to a cardiac focus of infection?
questions.explanation: Physical exam: vital signs, pallor, focus of infection (respiratory: tonsils, lungs; cardiac: heart murmur), rash, joints, lymph nodes, hepatosplenomegaly, masses, petechiae, dysmorphic features. A: Points to a marrow disorder. B: Not cardiac. C: Bleeding sign. E: Congenital disorder.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with fever has a WBC of 18,000/µL with neutrophilia and a new heart murmur. Which test is most useful next?
questions.explanation: Infection suspected: viral titers, cultures for bacteria, stool for parasites, chest X-ray, cardiac echo. A new murmur with fever points to a cardiac source. A: Malignancy work-up. B: Allergy work-up. D: Allergy work-up. E: Malignancy work-up.

questions.stem: A healthy 35-year-old who smokes 30 cigarettes a day has a WBC of 12,000/µL with neutrophilia on a routine check. Examination and smear are normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Causes of leukocytosis: infections, inflammation, drugs, marrow disorders, immune disorders; others include exercise, pregnancy, smoking, asplenia, stress, trauma and hemolysis. B: Smear and exam are normal. C: Early childhood infections. D: A cause is evident. E: Well, with no focus.

questions.stem: Which finding in a patient with leukocytosis most suggests a primary bone marrow disorder?
questions.explanation: Suspect a marrow disorder with weight loss, bleeding or bruising, pallor, recurrent life-threatening infections, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, a very high WBC, abnormal RBC or platelet counts, or blasts on the smear. A: Left shift of infection. C: Often reactive. D: A benign cause. E: EBV.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old has weight loss, easy bruising and splenomegaly. WBC 60,000/µL, Hb 8 g/dL, platelets 40,000/µL. What is the most useful next test?
questions.explanation: Weight loss, bruising, splenomegaly, a very high WBC and abnormal RBC and platelet counts suggest a marrow disorder. Malignancy suspected: bone marrow exam ± imaging, flow cytometry, cytogenetics, molecular studies. A: Infection work-up. B: Allergy work-up. C: Inflammation work-up. D: Parasite work-up.

questions.stem: Which patient with leukocytosis needs emergency care?
questions.explanation: Leukocytosis is an emergency with clinical instability (hypotension, high fever, hypothermia, rebound tenderness), blasts and DIC, or a WBC > 100,000/µL. A: A responding marrow. B: Benign. C: Mononucleosis; self-limited. E: Benign.

questions.stem: Which type of neutrophilia is most common?
questions.explanation: Neutrophilia (> 7,500/µL): secondary or reactive is most common (infections, inflammation, drugs, immune). Marrow causes: myeloproliferative disorders, hereditary neutrophilia (LAD), chronic idiopathic neutrophilia. A: A marrow disorder. B: Rare. D: No cause found. E: Malignant and rare.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has had cough and fever for 1 day, with tachypnea, grunting and decreased breath sounds. WBC 34,000/µL, neutrophils 73%, bands 8%. What do the counts indicate?

options.B: Marrow infiltration by acute leukemic blasts
options.E: A responding marrow in bacterial infection

questions.explanation: Marked leukocytosis and neutrophilia indicate severe bacterial infection with an excellent immune response. Raised bands = left shift and a responding marrow. Prognosis was excellent; symptoms resolved in 48 hours. A: WBC is below 50,000/µL. B: No blasts. C: Bands point to bacteria. D: First infection, short history.

questions.stem: In a child with bacterial pneumonia, what is a raised band count on the smear called?
questions.explanation: An increased band count indicates bacterial infection, a left shift and a responding marrow. B: WBC > 50,000/µL. C: Needs nucleated red cells. D: Seen in congenital neutropenia. E: Sludging in leukemia.

questions.stem: An unvaccinated 5-year-old has had 2 weeks of paroxysmal cough with an inspiratory whoop. WBC 28,000/µL, 78% small lymphocytes. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Selected bacteria cause lymphocytosis (> 4,000/µL): pertussis, tuberculosis, brucellosis, syphilis. A: Atypical lymphocytes and sore throat. B: Causes neutropenia. D: Neutrophilia. E: Neutrophilia.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old has WBC 48,000/µL with 88% small mature lymphocytes, Hb 9.5 g/dL, platelets 85,000/µL and splenomegaly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia: elderly patient with lymphocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia or neutropenia, and splenomegaly. A: Young adults; atypical lymphocytes. B: Children with cough. C: Neutrophils from a non-leukemic cause. E: A myeloid neoplasm.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of lymphocytosis?
questions.explanation: Causes of lymphocytosis: infections (viral most common; selected bacteria; parasites), malignancy (CLL, occasionally NHL), and others (stress, drugs, asplenia). A: Only selected ones. C: Less common. D: An occasional cause. E: Toxoplasmosis, malaria.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old has had 5 days of fever, sore throat and marked fatigue with no response to an antibiotic. She has exudates on both tonsils and splenomegaly. WBC 35,000/µL, 75% lymphocytes. What will the blood smear most likely show?
questions.explanation: Infectious mononucleosis (acute EBV infection) in adolescents and young adults: fever, fatigue, sore throat, exudative tonsillitis, splenomegaly; high WBC with atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells) on the smear. A: Leukemia. B: Chediak-Higashi syndrome. C: Leukoerythroblastic reaction. E: Bacterial infection.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old with exudative tonsillitis, splenomegaly and many atypical lymphocytes is suspected of infectious mononucleosis. Which test confirms it?
questions.explanation: Lab findings in infectious mononucleosis: high WBC, atypical lymphocytes on the smear, positive EBV-specific antibody test. A: Not needed. B: Malignancy work-up. D: Bacteria. E: Allergy work-up.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old has confirmed acute EBV infection with sore throat, fatigue and splenomegaly. What is the treatment?
questions.explanation: Infectious mononucleosis is usually self-limited; treatment is supportive. B: Viral illness. C: Not indicated. D: No neutropenia. E: Not a malignancy.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl with eczema and recurrent cough since early childhood has had dyspnea and dry cough for 8 hours. She has expiratory wheezes and poor air entry. WBC 10,000/µL, eosinophils 20%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Typical history and exam with eosinophilia (2,000/µL, above 500/µL) point to asthma. A: Lymphocytosis. B: Neutrophilia with bands. C: Does not fit the history. D: Atypical lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old farm worker with no allergies has a WBC of 9,000/µL with 15% eosinophils. Which cause should be looked for first?
questions.explanation: Absolute eosinophils 1,350/µL (> 500/µL) = eosinophilia, caused by allergies, parasitic infestations and some cancers. Stool for parasites when parasites are suspected. A: Lymphocytosis. C: Eosinopenia. D: Eosinopenia. E: Neutropenia.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with eczema and seasonal sneezing has eosinophilia. Which tests are most useful?

options.C: Serum IgE and skin prick tests

questions.explanation: Allergies suspected: IgE, skin prick tests. A: Parasite work-up. B: Infection work-up. D: Inflammation work-up. E: Malignancy work-up.

questions.stem: Basophilia is seen in which condition?
questions.explanation: Basophilia (> 200/µL): allergies, inflammation and myeloproliferative disorders. Monocytosis (> 800/µL): infections, inflammation, rarely cancer. A: Basopenia. B: Basopenia. C: Basopenia. E: Neutropenia.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old has WBC 2,800/µL: neutrophils 25%, lymphocytes 60%, monocytes 10%, eosinophils 4%, basophils 1%. Which cell line explains the leukopenia?
questions.explanation: ANC = 700/µL (moderate neutropenia). Neutropenia is the major cause of leukopenia; causes include infections, drugs, bone marrow failure and immune disorders. B: 1,680/µL, above 1,500. C: 280/µL, above 200. D: 112/µL, above 40. E: Too few to change the total.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old with a large hemangioma has an ANC of 0.8 ×10⁹/L. What is the mechanism of the neutropenia?
questions.explanation: Neutropenia mechanisms: decreased production; increased destruction (infections, drugs, immune); sequestration (splenic, large hemangiomas); shift from the circulating to the marginating pool. A: Drugs, infections, marrow failure. B: SLE, RA, alloimmune. C: Endotoxin, dialysis, bypass. D: Congenital neutropenia.

questions.stem: A woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has an isolated ANC of 0.9 ×10⁹/L. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: Immune causes (SLE, rheumatoid arthritis, neonatal alloimmune) increase neutrophil destruction. A: Drugs, irradiation, marrow failure. C: Spleen, hemangiomas. D: Endotoxin, dialysis, bypass. E: Congenital neutropenia.

questions.stem: How is neutropenia usually first suspected?
questions.explanation: Neutropenia itself has no symptoms; it is not suspected unless the patient has frequent or unusual infections. A: Anemia. B: Low platelets. C: Marrow disease. E: Not the usual clue.

questions.stem: A patient with an ANC of 0.2 ×10⁹/L is most likely to report which symptom?
questions.explanation: Severe neutropenia: fatigue, sleeplessness, restlessness, headache, high fever and chills, sore mouth and throat, skin and visceral infections, abscesses. A: Not a neutropenia symptom. B: Low platelets. C: Not a neutropenia symptom. D: Hemolysis.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old has a WBC of 2,000/µL with 30% neutrophils. How is the neutropenia classified?
questions.explanation: ANC = 2,000 × 0.30 = 600/µL (0.6 ×10⁹/L): moderate (0.5–1.0). Mild 1.0–2.0, severe < 0.5, agranulocytosis < 0.1 ×10⁹/L. A: ANC 1,000–2,000/µL. C: ANC < 500/µL. D: ANC < 100/µL. E: 600/µL is low.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old has a WBC of 1,500/µL with 5% neutrophils. How is this classified?
questions.explanation: ANC = 1,500 × 0.05 = 75/µL (< 0.1 ×10⁹/L): agranulocytosis, with life-threatening infections (hemodynamic instability, DIC). B: ANC < 500/µL but ≥ 100. C: ANC 500–1,000/µL. D: ANC 1,000–2,000/µL. E: Lymphocytes not given.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old who often eats at low-resource restaurants and is behind on vaccines has 5 days of high fever, diarrhea, abdominal pain and headache. His spleen is 3 cm below the costal margin. Hb 10 g/dL, WBC 4.0 ×10⁹/L, ANC 1.4 ×10⁹/L, platelets 90 ×10⁹/L. Blood culture grows gram-negative bacilli. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Typical presentation of typhoid fever; salmonella is among the bacteria that cause neutropenia (with brucella, shigella and tuberculosis). A: Intracellular; not grown in routine culture. B: A parasite. D: A virus. E: Not a gram-negative bacillus.

questions.stem: A man with typhoid fever has a WBC of 4.0 ×10⁹/L and an ANC of 1.4 ×10⁹/L. How is his neutropenia classified?
questions.explanation: ANC 1.4 ×10⁹/L lies in the mild range (1.0–2.0 ×10⁹/L). A: ANC 0.5–1.0. C: ANC < 0.5. D: ANC < 0.1. E: Below 2.0 is neutropenia.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 6-year-old has had fever and cough from influenza for 3 days. His ANC is 1.2 ×10⁹/L. A CBC last year was normal and he has never had a serious infection. What best explains the neutropenia?
questions.explanation: Many viruses (HIV, CMV, EBV, HPV, RSV, parvovirus B19, hepatitis, influenza, herpes, measles, rubella, varicella), bacteria (salmonella, brucella, shigella, TB), rickettsia and malaria cause neutropenia. The key question is whether infection is due to neutropenia or neutropenia is due to infection; a normal earlier CBC and no past infections favor the second. A: Early, severe and persistent. B: A diagnosis of exclusion. C: Leukocytosis. E: Newborns.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old who has felt low for a month started a pill that improved her mood. She now has 5 days of fever, fatigue and stomatitis. WBC 0.6 ×10⁹/L, ANC 0.3 ×10⁹/L, Hb, platelets and red cell indices normal; 10 days later the ANC is 0.2 ×10⁹/L. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Isolated severe neutropenia that persists after a new drug, with normal Hb, platelets and indices, is drug-induced. Drug-induced neutropenia is very frequent, ranges from mild to agranulocytosis, and is dose-related or idiosyncratic. A: Hb and red cell indices are normal. B: Transient; would not persist. C: Hb and platelets are normal. D: A cause is evident.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old taking an antithyroid drug for Graves disease develops fever and an ANC of 0.1 ×10⁹/L. Which mechanism is usually responsible?

options.B: Dose-related marrow aplasia from the drug

questions.explanation: Drug mechanisms: marrow depression (chemotherapy, ionizing radiation); impaired DNA synthesis (phenothiazines, chloramphenicol, hydroxyurea, chemotherapy); immunologic, usually complement-mediated (antithyroid drugs, sulfas, NSAIDs); idiosyncratic (chloramphenicol, antipsychotics, diuretics, sulfas, antimalarials). A: Phenothiazines, chloramphenicol, hydroxyurea. B: Chemotherapy, radiation. D: Not a drug mechanism. E: Not a drug mechanism.

questions.stem: A man taking hydroxyurea develops mild neutropenia. By which mechanism does the drug lower the count?
questions.explanation: Impairment of DNA synthesis: phenothiazines, chloramphenicol, hydroxyurea and chemotherapy. B: Antithyroid drugs, sulfas, NSAIDs. C: Not a drug mechanism. D: Not a drug mechanism. E: Congenital neutropenia.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old develops neutropenia after starting a sulfa antibiotic. She is afebrile and well. Besides stopping the drug, what is most important?
questions.explanation: Drug-related neutropenia: stop the drug and teach the patient to consult urgently for fever, mouth sores or other mucosal ulcers. A: Autoimmune neutropenia. B: Sequestration. C: Not needed while well. E: Marrow failure or congenital disease.

questions.stem: A 1-week-old girl of first-degree consanguineous parents has periorbital cellulitis with Staphylococcus aureus in the blood. ANC is 0 ×10⁹/L; Hb and platelets are normal. The cellulitis clears with IV antibiotics, but the ANC stays at 0 over 2 weeks. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: Persistent absent neutrophils from birth with a severe infection and consanguinity: a bone marrow aspirate shows maturation arrest at the promyelocyte–myelocyte stage (severe congenital neutropenia). A: The cellulitis has resolved. B: Sequestration. D: Autoimmune neutropenia. E: Persistent ANC 0 needs an answer now.

questions.stem: A newborn with a persistent ANC below 0.2 ×10⁹/L has a bone marrow aspirate. Which finding supports severe congenital neutropenia?
questions.explanation: Severe congenital neutropenia: severe decrease in neutrophils (< 0.5 to < 0.2 ×10⁹/L) and maturation arrest at the promyelocyte–myelocyte stage. A: One stage too early. B: Leukemia. C: Marrow failure. D: Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

questions.stem: Which gene is mutated in most cases of severe congenital neutropenia?
questions.explanation: Inheritance is variable, with the neutrophil elastase 2 gene (ELA2) the offending gene in most cases. B: LAD I. C: Chediak-Higashi syndrome. D: LAD II. E: LAD III.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with severe congenital neutropenia is followed long term. Which complication is he predisposed to?
questions.explanation: Severe congenital neutropenia: early life-threatening infections (sepsis, pneumonia, skin infections, oral ulcers, gingivitis) and a predisposition to leukemia. A: Chronic granulomatous disease. C: Chediak-Higashi syndrome. D: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency. E: LAD III.

questions.stem: Which treatment is used in severe congenital neutropenia?
questions.explanation: Treatment of severe congenital neutropenia: G-CSF and stem cell transplant. B: Autoimmune neutropenia. C: Sequestration. D: Not a treatment of SCN. E: Cause neutropenia.

questions.stem: A well-looking term newborn has omphalitis on day 5. ANC 0.2 ×10⁹/L, Hb and platelets normal. The mother is healthy with a normal CBC, and her serum reacts with the father's neutrophils. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Neonatal alloimmune neutropenia: transplacental passage of maternal IgG antibodies to neutrophil-specific antigens inherited from the father. A: The baby's own autoantibodies. B: Marrow maturation arrest. C: No cause found. D: No drug exposure.

questions.stem: What is the most likely cause of isolated neutropenia?
questions.explanation: Immune neutropenia is the most likely cause of isolated neutropenia; it is antibody or cytotoxic T cell related and can involve the marrow myeloid reserve, with a significant infection risk. A: Rare. B: Must be excluded but less common. C: Less common. E: Affects other lines too.

questions.stem: In immune neutropenia, how are antibody-coated neutrophils removed?

options.C: Sludging of neutrophils in small blood vessels

questions.explanation: Anti-neutrophil antibody → neutrophil-antibody complex → uptake and destruction by the RE system. A: Reversible; not destruction. C: Leukostasis. D: Congenital neutropenia. E: Sequestration.

questions.stem: A woman with a collagen vascular disease has autoimmune neutropenia and recurrent infections. Which treatment targets the cause?
questions.explanation: Autoimmune neutropenia (granulocyte-specific autoantibodies; with infections, collagen vascular disease, immune deficiencies) is treated with immunosuppressive therapy. A: Sequestration. B: Do not target the cause. D: Marrow failure or congenital disease. E: Drug-related neutropenia.

questions.stem: During hemodialysis, a patient's neutrophil count falls sharply and recovers after the session. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: Neutropenia from a shift from the circulating to the marginating pool: severe infection or endotoxin release, hemodialysis, cardiopulmonary bypass. A: Antibodies. B: Spleen. C: Too fast. D: Antithyroid drugs, sulfas, NSAIDs.

questions.stem: After cardiopulmonary bypass, a man has a transient fall in his neutrophil count and is otherwise well. What treatment is needed?
questions.explanation: Cardiopulmonary bypass shifts neutrophils to the marginating pool; marginating neutropenia needs no treatment. A: Not needed. B: He is well. C: Not immune. E: Not sequestration.

questions.stem: A woman with an ANC of 0.2 ×10⁹/L has a temperature of 39.5 °C, chills and a blood pressure of 85/50 mmHg. What is the best immediate management?

options.C: A bone marrow aspirate before any treatment

questions.explanation: Fever and septic symptoms in neutropenia: urgent hospitalization, broad-spectrum antibiotics, cultures, blood products and G-CSF. B: Septic; needs admission. C: Delays treatment. D: Septic; needs admission. E: Not the emergency step.

questions.stem: A child has severe, recurrent neutropenia from splenic sequestration. Which treatment is indicated?
questions.explanation: Sequestration: surgery in severe and recurrent cases. A: Do not remove the cause. C: Autoimmune. D: Marrow failure or congenital disease. E: Severe and recurrent.

questions.stem: A well 30-year-old has an ANC of 1.6 ×10⁹/L on a routine CBC. He has no infections and a normal examination. What is the best management?
questions.explanation: In most cases neutropenia needs no treatment; most WBC disorders are benign and self-limiting. Treatment depends on the cause. A: Not needed. B: No infection. D: Not indicated. E: Not indicated.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old has persistent unexplained neutropenia with no drug exposure, infection or autoimmune disease. Which condition must be excluded before calling it chronic idiopathic neutropenia?
questions.explanation: In unexplained neutropenia, exclude primary marrow disease (myelodysplastic syndrome, marrow infiltration); chronic idiopathic neutropenia is a diagnosis of exclusion. B: Not a cause of neutropenia. C: Basopenia. D: Childhood leukocytosis. E: Lymphocytosis.

questions.stem: In a child, lymphopenia is a lymphocyte count below what value?
questions.explanation: Lymphopenia: < 1.5 ×10⁹/L in adults, < 3.0 ×10⁹/L in children. A: The adult cut-off. C: The lymphocytosis cut-off in adults. D: Too low. E: Too low.

questions.stem: Besides immune deficiencies, what is the other major cause of lymphopenia?
questions.explanation: Major causes of lymphopenia: immune deficiencies and malnutrition. Other causes: steroids, chemotherapy, marrow failure, chronic infections (TB), malignancy (Hodgkin lymphoma). A: A less common cause. B: A less common cause. C: A less common cause. D: A less common cause.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy has recurrent ear discharge, diarrhea and failure to thrive. Weight and height are below the 3rd percentile, and tonsils and lymph nodes are absent. Lymphocyte count 1.8 ×10⁹/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Recurrent infections, failure to thrive, absent tonsils and lymph nodes and lymphopenia (< 3.0 ×10⁹/L in a child): severe combined immunodeficiency. A: Normal lymphocytes; granulomas. B: Leukocytosis. C: Low neutrophils. E: Albinism; giant granules.

questions.stem: Two days after starting high-dose prednisone, which change in the white cell differential is expected?
questions.explanation: Eosinopenia: acute stress, acute inflammation, corticosteroids. Basopenia also follows corticosteroids, and monocytopenia appears in the first hours after prednisone. A: Steroids cause basopenia. B: Steroids lower monocytes. D: Steroids cause lymphopenia. E: Not a steroid effect.

questions.stem: Basopenia is associated with which endocrine disorder?
questions.explanation: Basopenia: corticosteroids, stress, acute inflammation, hyperthyroidism, acute hypersensitivity reactions and infections. B: Not listed. C: Not listed. D: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: A child has chronic skin infections that heal with scarring, indolent lymph node infections and low-grade fevers; cultures are often negative. The neutrophil count is normal. Which category fits best?

options.E: A shift to the marginating pool

questions.explanation: Neutrophil dysfunction: chronic recurrent skin and mucosal infections, omphalitis, scarring; indolent infections in nodes, lungs or liver; overt sepsis rarer than in severe neutropenia; low-grade fevers with organisms that are hard to culture. A: The count is normal. C: WBC > 50,000/µL. D: Viral and opportunistic infections. E: Lowers the count briefly.

questions.stem: A 5-week-old boy still has his umbilical cord attached and now has omphalitis without pus. WBC 45,000/µL, mostly neutrophils. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: LAD (rare, autosomal recessive): early recurrent severe bacterial infections, delayed umbilical cord separation, poor wound healing and leukocytosis; defective migration means abscesses do not form. A: Killing defect; granulomas. B: Albinism; giant granules. D: Neutrophils are absent. E: Neutrophils are low.

questions.stem: What is the molecular defect in leukocyte adhesion deficiency type I?
questions.explanation: LAD I: neutrophils lack β2 integrins (ITGB2 mutation; absent or defective CD18/11). LAD II: no selectin ligands. LAD III: β integrin dysfunction in leukocytes and platelets. A: LAD II. B: Chronic granulomatous disease. C: Chediak-Higashi syndrome. E: Severe congenital neutropenia.

questions.stem: A child with recurrent bacterial infections and leukocytosis has neutrophils that cannot roll on the endothelium. Integrin expression is normal. Which molecule is most likely missing?
questions.explanation: Rolling depends on selectins on the endothelium binding their ligands on the neutrophil. LAD II: neutrophils lack ligands for selectins (SLC35C1 mutation). A: Expression is normal. B: Killing, not rolling. C: Granule fusion. D: Congenital neutropenia.

questions.stem: A child with leukocytosis and delayed umbilical cord separation has recurrent severe bacterial infections and also prolonged mucosal bleeding with a normal platelet count. Which disorder is most likely?
questions.explanation: LAD III: leukocytes and platelets lack functioning β integrins (FERMT3 mutation), causing both leukocyte and platelet dysfunction. A: No platelet defect. C: No platelet defect. D: Albinism; no leukocytosis. E: No bleeding defect.

questions.stem: What is the curative treatment of leukocyte adhesion deficiency?
questions.explanation: LAD treatment: antibiotics and stem cell transplant. A: Neutrophils are already high. B: Not immune. C: Not sequestration. E: Not curative.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with light skin and hair has recurrent skin infections and blinks a lot in the sun. The CBC is normal; the smear shows large granules in the cytoplasm of every white cell type. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Chediak-Higashi syndrome: rare autosomal recessive granule fusion defect of leukocytes, nerve endings and melanocytes → partial albinism, nystagmus, defective chemotaxis and killing; very large leukocyte granules. B: Normal granules; granulomas. C: Leukocytosis. D: Absent neutrophils. E: No giant granules.

questions.stem: In Chediak-Higashi syndrome, the defective protein regulates which process?
questions.explanation: A defective CHS1/LYST gene encodes the lysosomal trafficking regulator protein, leading to defective lysosomal function. A: Chronic granulomatous disease. B: LAD I. D: LAD II. E: Severe congenital neutropenia.

questions.stem: A child with partial albinism, nystagmus and giant leukocyte granules bleeds heavily after a tooth extraction. The platelet count is normal. What explains the bleeding?
questions.explanation: Chediak-Higashi syndrome: platelets lack dense granules and have abnormal function; some patients also have mild to moderate neutropenia. Treatment: stem cell transplant. A: LAD III. B: Hemophilia A. C: von Willebrand disease. D: The count is normal.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy has had Aspergillus pneumonia and a Serratia infection, with granulomas on biopsy and poor growth. His neutrophil count is normal. Which defect is most likely?
questions.explanation: Chronic granulomatous disease: severe recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, unusual microbes (Serratia, Nocardia, Aspergillus, Pseudomonas), granulomas, growth retardation; mutations in phagocytic NADPH oxidase. B: LAD; leukocytosis. C: Chediak-Higashi syndrome. D: Neutropenia. E: LAD II.

questions.stem: Phagocytes in chronic granulomatous disease fail to produce which molecule?
questions.explanation: Mutations in phagocytic NADPH oxidase lead to failure of superoxide production, so phagocytes cannot kill the microbes they ingest. A: Mutated in congenital neutropenia. B: Not the defect. C: Specific granule protein. D: LAD II.

questions.stem: Which test establishes a suspected diagnosis of chronic granulomatous disease?
questions.explanation: CGD diagnosis: neutrophil function testing and mutation analysis. A: Congenital neutropenia. B: LAD. C: Chediak-Higashi syndrome. E: Infectious mononucleosis.

questions.stem: A boy with chronic granulomatous disease is well between infections. What is the main long-term measure?
questions.explanation: CGD treatment: early diagnosis and treatment of infections, lifelong antimicrobial prophylaxis, HSCT for high-risk patients. A: Neutrophils are normal in number. B: Sequestration. D: Not immune. E: Not enough.

questions.stem: Hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome is a defect of which neutrophil function?
questions.explanation: Chemotactic defects: LAD I, Chediak-Higashi syndrome, hyper-IgE (Job) syndrome, actin polymerization defect, localized aggressive periodontitis, acquired motility defects. A: LAD I and II. C: LAD I, actin defects. D: CGD, specific granule deficiency. E: Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
